newsitem.title: USA: Pickup in CBOs seen supporting US junk bond market.
newsitem.headline: Pickup in CBOs seen supporting US junk bond market.

text.p: An expected pickup in issuance of collateralized bond obligations (CBOs) backed by high-yield debt may help to support prices following the recent correction in the junk bond market, players said.

"CBOs have been an important factor all along in supporting high-yield prices. They may provide an important source of demand if mutual funds continue to exit the market," said Martin Fridson, chief high-yield strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.
Demand for junk bonds from the growing number of CBO issuers is increasingly being viewed as a type of "automatic stablizer" to junk bond prices during a downturn, market players said.

The total amount of new CBOs is expected to increase to between $8.0 billion and $10 billion in 1997 from $6.5 billion in 1996 as demand for these securities increases, said Sam DeRosa-Farag, director of high-yield strategy at Chase Securities Inc.
That amount could increase, he notes, if prices for junk bonds continue to fall.

In a typical CBO, an issuer will buy a large amount of junk bonds, bank loans or emerging market debt in the market, place them in a trust, and issue asset-backed-securities (ABS) backed by the cash flow generated from the assets, as well as equity.
The arbitrage between the price of underlying collateral and the price of investment-grade ABS is an important factor that makes the deals economically feasible, experts noted.

The recent correction in the junk bond market has improved the arbitrage, making conditions for issuing new CBOs more attractive, said Philip Seefried, managing director and head of high-yield sales and trading as Credit Suisse First Boston.
Analysts noted spreads of high-yield bonds have widened by some 44 basis points in the past three weeks, while those of ABS have remained relatively unchanged.
Seefried added that other factors were at work that make the current market even more attractive for CBO deals.

"In the last three to four weeks the new-issue market has been coming cheap to the secondary market. That is a wonderful source of collateral for CBOs because they are priced at par or at a discount and have no accrued interest," said Seefried.
He noted the pickup in mutual fund redemptions was another important fuel source for new CBOs.
"Mutual funds tend to own single-B bonds and if they are forced to sell, the natural buyers could be CBOs," he added.
"To the extent (CBO growth) occurs, then obviously you will have some demand offsetting the bleeding in mutual funds," said Chase's DeRosa-Farag.
But DeRosa-Farag said that the effect of rising CBO issuance on the junk market was primarily "psychological."
He said, "The main reason...the market is going through a correction is driven by fundamentals. Little of that can be offset through CBOs."
DeRosa-Farag added CBO managers do not tend to be large buyers of zero coupon bonds, the sector that has been hit hardest during the recent sell-off.

William Ficca, director of research at CONSECO Capital Managment, said: "Generic (junk bond) names will be buoyed a bit, but CBOs won't come in and save the (telecommunication) paging sector. CBO managers will not be buying names whose near-term prospects are not encouraging."
Market players also noted that while conditions for these transactions have improved, it is difficult to "market-time" a CBO because they are complex and often take several months to put together.

Nevertheless, the recent sell-off in the junk bond market was expected to accelerate CBO deals in progress and draw potential issuers, who have previously been discouraged by tight spreads, back into the market, they said.
An announcement by TCW Group last week that it raised $1.05 billion to create the second largest high-yield investment fund ever, also helped to fuel this perception, they said.

"I sense a lot more new kickoffs, requests for presentations and new deals getting started," said a high-yield official. "I suspect that means in a couple of weeks time, you might see two to three deals come out relatively quickly."
((-- U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1662))
